title: Iran widens Gulf attacks after US strikes missile launch site | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

Iran targeted a Kuwaiti air base that hosts US forces on Wednesday, widening the scope of its attacks after the US military hit what it said was a missile launch site in Iran.

Iran’s army targeted Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait with drones, state-run Press TV reported. The Kuwaiti Army’s General Staff said any explosions heard were caused by air defense systems intercepting incoming attacks.

Neighboring Bahrain, which is home to the US Fifth Fleet and has facedrepeated Iranian attacksover the past week, also sounded air raid sirens early Wednesday, with the military saying it had intercepted “a number of Iranian aerial attacks” early Wednesday.

CNN has contacted the US Central Command (CENTCOM) for comment.

Just hours earlier, US fighter jets carried out a “self-defense” strike against an Iranian missile launch site on Qeshm Island using “precision munitions,” according to an American military official.

The strike “was in response to IRGC aggression targeting American personnel and assets,” the official said, noting that CENTCOM remains “highly vigilant and fully postured to protect Americans across the region.”

Iranian state media reported that an area on the outskirts of a city on Qeshm Island had been targeted in an “enemy attack.” Ahmad Nafisi, the deputy governor of Hormozgan province for political and security affairs, said the strike caused no damage to vital infrastructure, commercial or residential areas.

Iran’s widening attacks come as Tehran warns it will not accept a prolonged stalemate in its war with the US, while President Donald Trump has signaled a preference for maintaining crippling economic pressure on the Islamic Republic rather than resuming full-scale hostilities. Iran has also threatened to expand the war significantly and warned that it will not wait for another US attack before striking.

Tuesday’s US strikesappear similar to othersin recent weeks around the Strait of Hormuz, which US officials have also characterized as defensive, rather than marking a significant escalation by American forces.

A third US aircraft carrier strike group recently entered CENTCOM’s area of responsibility, where it is expected to — at least temporarily — join ongoing operations that include enforcing a blockade of Iranian ports and conducting escort operations for commercial ships willing to transit the Strait.

Attacks on oil and gas tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz have surged in recent weeks. On Wednesday, the United Arab Emirates’ state-owned ADNOC energy company said one of its vessels had been attacked while transiting the waterway the previous evening, leaving 11 crew members injured and one missing.

“Today’s developments should serve as an important reminder of the inherent instability of the current situation,” Hamidreza Azizi, an Iran analyst at Crisis Group, wrote on X. “Some within the Trump administration – and perhaps even Trump himself – may believe that Washington can maintain economic pressure and the naval blockade against Iran indefinitely while avoiding another full-scale war. But the developments of the past 24 hours demonstrate how difficult it is to sustain such an arrangement.”

There is little indication of an imminent diplomatic agreement to end the conflict, and Trump has warned he could resume full combat operations if Tehran refuses to accept the US administration’s demands.

Trump was widely expected to hold off on restarting those combat operations until after the US midterm elections but appears to still be mulling over how to proceed, absent a last-minute deal.

With Democrats poised to take control of the House and Senate in January, Trump’s window to decide on a path forward in Iran appears to be shrinking. CNN has previously reported that it is likely untenable for the US military to maintain the status quo indefinitely, but only Trump has the power to decide when the war is over.

CNN’s Abbas Al Lawati, Lucas Lilieholm and Mohammed Tawfeeq contributed reporting.

CNN’s Abbas Al Lawati, Lucas Lilieholm and Mohammed Tawfeeq contributed reporting.
